vignette:
During the second year of the civil war, Amina was in the central market of her hometown, buying vegetables for dinner. The explosion came without warning-a blast wave that lifted her off her feet and threw her against a concrete pillar. She remembers the sound less as noise and more as a physical force that pressed through her chest. When the ringing in her ears faded, she heard screaming. Blood streaked her arms from a deep gash on her elbow, but she does not remember feeling pain. Instead, she remembers the stillness of a child's sandal lying a few feet away, separated from its owner.

Amina made her way home through broken glass, weaving through bodies and rubble. Her husband found her an hour later, sitting in the kitchen, still clutching the empty shopping bag. She did not speak about what she saw. That night, she lay awake, her body taut, listening for sounds that were not there.

In the months that followed, Amina buried herself in her work. She managed large infrastructure projects for a construction firm in her new country, where she and her husband had resettled. She needed to keep busy-every minute accounted for, every risk mapped out in spreadsheets and contingency plans. She became known as a micromanager, double-checking every contractor's timeline, demanding weekly progress reports and daily status updates. Her team complained that she never let go of control. But Amina felt that if she relaxed for even a second, something catastrophic would slip through.

She avoids the city center now. The weekly grocery run she once enjoyed has become a tactical operation: she goes only at off-peak hours, takes the perimeter aisles, keeps her back to the wall. Her husband does the shopping for big events-holidays, family dinners-because Amina cannot handle the noise of a crowded market. The smell of raw meat, the clatter of voices, the sudden shout of a vendor-they drop her straight back into that Tuesday afternoon, the air thick with dust and screams.

At night, her sleep is shallow. She wakes with a jolt, heart racing, convinced she has heard an explosion. Her husband's gentle hand on her shoulder sometimes helps, sometimes makes it worse-she does not want to be touched when she is coming out of the dream. She has stopped attending public celebrations. Her sister-in-law criticized her at a family gathering last month. "You're hiding," she said. Amina nodded. It was true.

Her attention at work has frayed at the edges. She spends hours re-reading emails, searching for hidden threats in a contractor's wording, second-guessing her own calculations. A minor delay sends a spike of dread through her. She cannot let go of the feeling that a disaster is just around the corner-not in some abstract, "something might go wrong" way, but in the visceral certainty that the floor will disappear beneath her feet.

Her husband has tried to talk with her, to pull her back into intimacy. But Amina feels as though a pane of glass sits between her and the rest of the world. She sees others laughing, planning vacations, arguing about small things-and she cannot connect. The old pleasure she took in hosting dinners, in walking through a construction site and visualizing the finished building, has become muted, like a sound turned down very low.

She came to therapy because her boss gave her an ultimatum after she missed three deadlines in two months. She sits on the edge of the chair, hands clasped, eyes scanning the room. She does not want to talk about the explosion. But she also does not want to keep living inside a body that will not stop bracing for a blow that already landed.
